chunks: Ali, from his father, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Hariz, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:
When you find a man during the agony of death, instruct him with the words of relief:

There is no god except Allah, the Forbearing, the Generous. There is no god except Allah, the Most High, the Magnificent. Glory be to Allah, Lord of the seven heavens and Lord of the seven earths and whatever is in them and whatever is between them and whatever is beneath them, and Lord of the Magnificent Throne; and all praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

He (the narrator) said: Then Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'Had I found Ikrima at the time of death, I would have benefited him.' It was said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'With what would he have benefited him?' He said: 'He would have instructed him with what you are upon (i.e., al-Wilayah).'

key_terms.النزع: The agony/death rattle — the final moments before death
key_terms.الولاية: Al-Wilayah — the divinely-ordained authority and guardianship of the Imam; the core of Shia doctrine
key_terms.تلقين: Talqeen — instructing/indoctrinating; reciting words to guide a person at the moment of death
key_terms.كلمات الفرج: Words of relief/deliverance — specific dhikr formulas recited to ease the passage of death

ai.seo_question: What dhikr should be recited to a dying person according to Imam al-Baqir in al-Kafi?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) instructs believers to recite specific dhikr formulas — the kalima of tawhid and glorification of God's dominion over all creation — to a dying person (talqeen). The addition of the story about Ikrima reveals the deeper significance: the ultimate benefit at death is instruction in the belief in al-Wilayah (the authority and guardianship of the Imams). The phrase 'what you are upon' refers to Shia belief in the Imamate, distinguishing it from mere verbal declaration of the shahada.
